Genealogy means the study and tracing of who came before you in your family — your parents, their parents, and all the ancestors going back as far as records allow. It is the careful, systematic process of discovering, documenting, and understanding where a person or a family comes from, generation by generation.

Think of your family as a tree. You are a leaf at the top. Your parents are the branch that holds you. Their parents are the branches behind them. And so on, all the way down to the roots deep in the ground. Genealogy is the study of that entire tree — every branch, every root, every connection.
Two Ways the Word Is Used

The word "genealogy" carries two closely related but distinct meanings, and both are correct:

1. Genealogy as a field of study / practice

Here, genealogy refers to the activity or discipline of researching and tracing family histories. Used this way, it is similar to how we use words like "history" or "science" — it names a subject of investigation.

"She has been passionate about genealogy for decades."
"Genealogy has become one of the most popular hobbies in the world."

2. A genealogy as a specific family record

Here, "a genealogy" (or "the genealogy of...") refers to a particular, documented account of one family's line of descent — basically, a family's story told through its members across generations. The plural form, genealogies, is used in this sense.

"The historian published a genealogy of the royal family."
"The library holds genealogies of many old families in the region."

Both meanings revolve around the same thing: family lineage across time.

Genealogy is not just knowing that your grandmother was born in a certain city. It is a detailed, evidence-based investigation. A person who practices genealogy — called a genealogist — works to answer questions like:

  • Who were my ancestors?
  • When and where were they born, married, and did they die?
  • Where did they live and migrate?
  • What were their occupations, cultures, and backgrounds?
  • How are different family members related to each other?

To answer these questions, genealogists study and gather evidence from a wide variety of sources, such as:

  • Birth, marriage, and death certificates
  • Census records (official population counts from the government)
  • Church and baptism records
  • Immigration and ship passenger records
  • Land ownership and property records
  • Military service records
  • Wills and probate documents
  • Old letters, diaries, and family photographs
  • Newspaper archives and obituaries
  • DNA testing, which can reveal biological relationships and ethnic origins

The work of genealogy is essentially detective work — piecing together clues from the past to build a reliable, accurate picture of a family's history.

The most recognizable result of genealogical research is a family tree — a diagram or chart that visually shows how family members across multiple generations are connected. Each person is a "node" on the tree, connected to their parents, children, and siblings.

However, genealogy can also be presented as:

  • A written narrative (a family history written like a story)
  • A pedigree chart (showing direct ancestors only — parents, grandparents, great-grandparents, etc.)
  • A descendant chart (showing all the people who descend from one ancestor)
  • A database or digital file, especially with modern genealogy software

It helps to know how genealogy relates to nearby ideas:

  • Family history is a broader, softer term that often includes stories, culture, traditions, and social context. Genealogy is more precise — it focuses specifically on lines of descent and biological/legal relationships.
  • Ancestry refers to the ancestors themselves (the people you descended from). Genealogy is the study of that ancestry.
  • Lineage refers to the direct line of descent from an ancestor to a descendant. Genealogy maps out lineages systematically.
Scope: How Far Can Genealogy Go?

Genealogy can operate on different scales:

  • Personal genealogy — tracing your own family's history
  • Family genealogy — tracing the history of a surname or clan
  • Royal/noble genealogy — documenting the lineage of ruling families, often for questions of inheritance or succession
  • Scientific/biological genealogy — using genetics and DNA to trace human ancestry, sometimes going back thousands of years to understand migration patterns of ancient peoples

People pursue genealogy for many deeply human reasons:

  • Identity and belonging — Understanding where you come from gives you a stronger sense of who you are.
  • Cultural connection — Tracing roots back to a specific country or ethnic group helps people reconnect with traditions, languages, and heritage.
  • Medical awareness — Knowing your family medical history can reveal inherited health conditions or genetic risks.
  • Legal purposes — Proving descent can matter for inheritance, citizenship claims, or tribal membership.
  • Historical interest — Some people want to understand how their family lived through major historical events — wars, migrations, famines, revolutions.
  • Simple curiosity — The timeless desire to know one's own story.
A Simple One-Sentence Definition to Remember

If you ever need to recall this word quickly:

Genealogy is the study and documentation of family lineage — who is related to whom, across generations — tracing back through ancestors as far as records allow.

Everything else about the word is just a deeper exploration of that one idea.
